_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Itself [not]: even though the offspring of the substitute is fit for sacrifice.
rashi:a1.2: What would he have answered him? [A line in Rashi’s text that is not in our printed Gemara.] That is, from his saying “I answer you forced answers, Babylonian style,” it follows that he knew another answer.
gershom:a1.1: What are we dealing with here? That he brings [a burnt offering] with their money, where [the offspring] is not fit for sacrifice, because she gave birth to a female.
gershom:a2.1: I answer you forced answers, Babylonian style, who bring an elephant through the eye of a needle: yes, our mishna deals with a case where she gave birth to a female, [and so on] until the end of the world.
gershom:a3.1: And if not for a forced answer [like this one], what could he have answered about it?
gershom:a4.1: He could have answered: what is taught, “their money goes to free-will offerings,” is when she gave birth to a female; but if she gave birth to a male, it is sacrificed as a burnt offering, as we said.
gershom:a5.1: [A note on the mishna of 20b.] But even in a free-will offering it is a burnt offering: what the Sages said, “their money goes to free-will offerings,” means a [burnt offering]. If so, what is the difference between the words of Rabbi Elazar and the Sages? Only this: when it comes as an obligation, as an individual’s free-will offering, as Rabbi Elazar says, it requires leaning [of hands] and libations from his own [means], like any individual’s offering; and if the one who brings it is a priest, its service and its hide are his. Even though it is not his priestly watch that is serving, he may sacrifice it and burn it, as it is written: “And he shall come with all the desire of his soul… and he shall minister” (Deuteronomy 18:6–7), and its hide is his, as it is written: “The hide of the burnt offering which he has offered shall be the priest’s, it shall be his” (Leviticus 7:8). But when it comes as a free-will offering for the communal free-will burnt offerings, he does not lean on it, since a communal offering does not require leaning, and he does not bring libations for it from his own but from the community’s. And even if the owner of this offspring of the substitute of a guilt offering is a priest, he cannot perform its service; rather, its service and its hide belong to the men of the serving watch.
rashi:a2.1: MISHNA. These are like a firstborn and a tithe animal: in all the sanctity of a firstborn and a tithe animal, that they are not sold in the butchers’ market after a blemish befell them and they were redeemed.
gershom:a6.1: And they are eaten in their blemish by the owners: without redemption, like a firstborn and a tithe animal, which have no redemption, since it is written of them “you shall not redeem” (Numbers 18:17) and “it shall not be redeemed” (Leviticus 27:33).
gershom:a7.1: For all sacrificial animals are sold in the butchers’ market: because their profit goes to the Temple treasury; except for the firstborn and the tithe animal, whose benefit goes to the owners. Therefore we do not treat them with disrespect.
rashi:a3.1: Except for the firstborn and the tithe animal: because the benefit from their sale does not go to the Temple treasury, since the money for a firstborn goes to the priest and the money for a tithe animal goes to the owners, and for the sake of their benefit we do not treat sacred things with disrespect.
rashi:a4.1: If a blemish befell a firstborn or a tithe animal, one cannot take them out of their sanctity, since of the firstborn it is written “you shall not redeem” (Numbers 18:17) and of the tithe animal it is written “it shall not be redeemed” (Leviticus 27:33).
rashi:a4.2: Except for the firstborn and the tithe animal: which do not come ab initio from outside the Land, as all other sacrificial animals do.
gershom:a8.1: And they come from outside the Land to the Land to be sacrificed, except for the firstborn and the tithe animal, which do not come; and even so, if they came unblemished, after the fact, the firstborn and tithe animal are sacrificed, and if blemished they are eaten by the owners without redemption. And Rabbi Shimon said: what is the reason a firstborn and a tithe animal do not come from outside the Land [ab initio]? Because a firstborn and a tithe animal have provision in their place: one can sustain them outside the Land until a permanent blemish befalls them, and as soon as a blemish befalls them one can eat them without redemption. Therefore one need not bring them up. But all other sacrificial animals have no such provision outside the Land, that they become permitted as soon as a blemish befalls them without redemption; rather, they require redemption. Therefore they remain in their sanctity and are more stringent than a firstborn and a tithe animal, and so they come from outside the Land.
rashi:a5.1: For the firstborn and the tithe animal have provision in their place: they have a remedy in their place, that they graze until they become blemished and are eaten in their blemish by the owners. But all other sacrificial animals, even though a blemish befell them, remain in their sanctity, and you must redeem them, bring up their money and sacrifice [with it]; and since in the end their money will be sacrificed, let them themselves be brought up and sacrificed.
rashi:a6.1: GEMARA. He is not liable: to lashes, on account of “there shall be no blemish in it” (Leviticus 22:21).
tosafot:a6.1: One who inflicts a blemish on the substitute of a firstborn or a tithe animal, what is the law? In the chapter Kol HaMenaḥot Ba’ot Matza (Menaḥot 56b) tanna’im disagree about one who inflicts a blemish on an animal that is already blemished: one says he is flogged and one says he is not. And this dilemma here arises according to both. Even according to the one who says there that he is flogged, that is because there the animal was fit for sacrifice before the blemish; but these, which are never fit for sacrifice, perhaps he is not flogged, or perhaps it makes no difference. And according to the one who says there that he is not flogged, that is because from the outset it already had a blemish; but here, where it was unblemished at the outset, perhaps he is flogged, or perhaps it makes no difference.
gershom:a9.1: One who inflicts a blemish on the substitute of a firstborn or a tithe animal, what is the law? [Their stringency, which we mentioned:] one who inflicts a blemish on [other] sacrificial animals transgresses five prohibitions. Here, what is the law? Do we say that since they are not sacrificed, as it is written “you shall not redeem; they are holy” (Numbers 18:17), “they” are sacrificed but their substitutes are not, and the tithe animal is derived from the firstborn by the verbal analogy of “passing” and “passing,” and therefore he is not liable? Or perhaps, since they are sanctified, as it is written “then it and its substitute shall be holy” (Leviticus 27:10), he is liable?
rashi:a7.1: And let the dilemma be raised about the ninth of the tithe: for example, where he called the ninth “tenth,” which is sacred but is not sacrificed, as we say at the end of Bekhorot (60a): the ninth is eaten in its blemish.
gershom:a10.1: And let the dilemma be raised about [one who inflicts a blemish on] the ninth of the tithe, which is not sacrificed, as we learned: if he called the ninth “tenth,” the tenth “ninth,” and the eleventh “tenth,” all three are consecrated; the ninth is eaten in its blemish by the owners, the tenth is the tithe animal, and the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering. But the ninth is not sacrificed. [Rather, what is different, and so on.]
rashi:a8.1: To exclude the ninth: that it is not sacrificed. And since it is not sacrificed, it is obvious to us that one who inflicts a blemish on it is not liable. Here too, and so on.
rashi:a12.1: Ben Antigonus, and they did not accept them from him: this is difficult for our mishna, which teaches: if they came unblemished, they are sacrificed.
gershom:a11.1: Ben Antigonus brought up firstborns and they did not accept them from him: even after the fact.
rashi:a12.2: This is Rabbi Yishmael, and so on: (it is explained below).
gershom:a12.1: It is not difficult: what it teaches, “if they came unblemished, they are sacrificed,” [is Rabbi Yishmael’s view], who below juxtaposes second tithe to the firstborn: just as a firstborn is eaten only in the presence of the Temple. It follows that even a firstborn from outside the Land is eaten in the presence of the Temple. And what it says, “they did not accept it from him,” [is] Rabbi Akiva’s view, who below juxtaposes the firstborn to second tithe: just as second tithe comes only from the Land, as it is written “you may not eat within your gates…” (Deuteronomy 12:17), so too a firstborn comes only from the Land.
rashi:a13.1: Three elders: Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva and ben Azzai.
gershom:a13.1: In the name of three elders: Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva and ben Azzai. A firstborn requires bringing to the place, as it is written: “And there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices…” (Deuteronomy 12:6). Just as a firstborn is eaten only in the presence of the Temple, when its blood was offered on the altar, so too [second] tithe is eaten only in the presence of the Temple, and when there is no Temple it is not eaten, even in Jerusalem. Let first fruits prove it: they have no placing of blood and sacrificial portions, yet they require bringing to the place, and tithe requires bringing to the place; just as first fruits are eaten only in the presence of the Temple, since it is written of them that they are set down beside the altar.
rashi:a14.1: A firstborn, tithe and first fruits require bringing to the place, as it is written: “And there you shall bring your burnt offerings… and the teruma of your hand” (Deuteronomy 12:5–6); these are the first fruits.
rashi:a14.2: Just as a firstborn is not eaten, and so on: as it explains below, since it requires placing the blood and sacrificial portions on the altar.
rashi:a15.1: First fruits are eaten only in the presence of the Temple: as it is written: “And you shall set it down before the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 26:10).
rashi:a16.1: Placement: before the altar, as it is written: “And you shall set it down before the Lord your God.”
rashi:a18.1: And let the inference return, and so on: why do I need a verse? Let the inference return and say: let the firstborn prove it, and the inference returns: the common element of them is that they require bringing to the place and are eaten only in the presence of the Temple; so too I will bring tithe [under that rule].
gershom:a14.1: And why does he need a verse to derive it? Let the inference return and come, and derive it by the common element, saying thus: since he said, “What about first fruits, which require placement?” let us say: let the firstborn prove it, which does not require placement, and I too will bring tithe. “What about the firstborn, which requires placing of blood?” Let first fruits prove it. And the inference returns: the aspect of this is not like the aspect of that, and so on. [Rav Ashi answers:] since they have an aspect of the altar, placement for first fruits and placing of blood for the firstborn; will you say so of second tithe, which has no aspect of the altar? Therefore a verse was needed to juxtapose [it] to tithe.
rashi:a20.1: And what does he hold? For it is obvious to him that a firstborn is not eaten, while second tithe is a doubt to him.
rashi:a20.2: And sanctified it for the future: both of them, firstborn and tithe, can be brought, and let them sacrifice it, since now too Jerusalem is sacred for sacrificing.
rashi:a20.3: And if it did not sanctify it for the future, and even so he is in doubt about tithe, let him be in doubt about the firstborn too. And why does he derive second tithe from the firstborn?
tosafot:a20.1: If he holds that the initial consecration sanctified for its time and sanctified for the future, let him bring a firstborn too: Rashi explained in Zevaḥim (107b) that according to the one who says it sanctified for the future, one may sacrifice even though there is no Temple. And if you ask: but we need an altar, and there is none? One can answer that it challenges from a firstborn that was slaughtered and whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple was destroyed, which lacks only eating within the wall, like tithe. Alternatively, one can answer that it challenges thus: let him bring a firstborn too and build an altar. “And if he holds it did not sanctify for the future, let him be in doubt about the firstborn too”: so Rashi reads. And it is difficult: according to the one who says it did not sanctify for the future, there is no more sanctity in Jerusalem than in other cities. And further, it says in the last chapter of Zevaḥim (ibid.) that according to the one who says it did not sanctify for the future, second tithe is eaten in all the cities of Israel. One can resolve at least the second difficulty: here it deals with tithe that was sown before the Temple was destroyed, which required bringing to Jerusalem, and of that it was not said that it is eaten in all the cities of Israel.
rashi:a21.1: Actually, it did not sanctify for the future: and as for your difficulty, what is different about the firstborn, that it is obvious to him? We are dealing with a firstborn like this, whose blood was sprinkled in the presence of the Temple and [the Temple] was destroyed, and so on; and he derives the meat from the blood: just as, if the blood were here now, it would not be sprinkled, since it did not sanctify for the future, so too the meat is not eaten.
tosafot:a21.1: Rashi reads thus: “Actually, he holds it did not sanctify for the future.” And it is difficult: if so, why do I need this reason, that the meat is juxtaposed to the blood? Derive it from the fact that it is disqualified by leaving [its area], since [Jerusalem] is like a place that has no wall. And further, it says in Zevaḥim (60a) that if the altar was damaged, one does not eat offerings of lesser sanctity on its account, and derives it from this very reason, that its meat is juxtaposed to its blood; while here it says that this juxtaposition of meat to blood is according to the one who says it did not sanctify for the future. Therefore it seems to the Ri that one reads: “If he holds it did not sanctify for the future, let him not bring second tithe” (with tithe sown before the Temple was destroyed, as we explained), and one reads: “Actually, he holds the initial consecration sanctified for its time and sanctified for the future; and as for your difficulty, let him bring a firstborn too: here we are dealing with one whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple, and the Temple was destroyed, and so on.” Now all the difficulties are resolved. And my teacher examined this: granted, a firstborn whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple is eaten only in the presence of the Temple, as the Gemara explains, because the meat is juxtaposed to the blood; but first fruits that had placement before the Temple, why are they eaten only in the presence of the Temple? And my teacher, Rabbi M. R. [so abbreviated in the text], said that indeed they may be eaten even in the present time, and where it says they are not eaten, it is where they had no placement before the Temple. And the matter proves it, since it challenges: “What about first fruits, which require placement?” And where it establishes the case as a firstborn that was slaughtered and whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple, that refers to the conclusion of the baraita, which juxtaposes tithe to the firstborn; presumably the firstborn is like tithe, which lacks only bringing to the place, that is, when its blood was sprinkled before the Temple. But the baraita speaks only of first fruits that were not set down; if they were set down before the Temple, it may be that they are eaten even after the destruction.
gershom:a15.1: And what does Rabbi Yishmael hold? If he holds like Rabbi Yehoshua, that the initial consecration that [Joshua] made sanctified also for the future, even after the destruction, then let him bring a firstborn too now in Jerusalem and eat it there.
gershom:a16.1: And if he holds that it did not sanctify [for the future], then even for tithe let him resolve that it is not brought.
gershom:a17.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads:] Ravina said: Actually, he holds the initial consecration sanctified for the future; and as for what you said, “if so, let him bring a firstborn too,” you cannot say so, for here we are dealing with a firstborn whose blood was sprinkled before the destruction of the Temple, and the Temple was destroyed, and its meat still exists. And he derives its meat from its blood: just as its blood was at the altar, so its meat at the altar. It required placing [the sacrificial portions] on the altar, and now that there is no altar it has no remedy and cannot be eaten. And he derives second tithe from this firstborn: it is not eaten even in Jerusalem, so too second tithe is not eaten, even though [the initial consecration] sanctified for the future. And since tithe is derived from the firstborn, all the more so are other firstborns derived from this firstborn.
rashi:b1.1: And tithe comes and is derived from the firstborn: through the juxtaposition of “And you shall eat before the Lord…” (Deuteronomy 14:23), where second tithe is juxtaposed to the firstborn. And since there is a firstborn about which it is obvious to him that it is eaten only in the presence of the Temple, such as this one, we derive tithe from it.
rashi:b1.2: And do we derive sacred things from one another? As here, where you derive meat from blood and tithe from meat.
rashi:b1.3: But doesn’t Rabbi Yoḥanan say, and so on: and the reason is explained in Eizehu Mekoman (Zevaḥim 49b).
rashi:b1.4: A derived thing from a derived thing: as here, where tithe is derived from meat, and the meat itself is derived from blood.
rashi:b2.1: It is non-sacred: and we derive it.
rashi:b2.2: We follow the derived: if it is non-sacred, we derive it from the teaching source.
rashi:b2.3: We follow the teaching source: the teaching source must be non-sacred.
rashi:b2.4: What is there to say? For the teaching source is the firstborn. It is difficult for me: since [the initial consecration] did not sanctify for the future, why is he in doubt about tithe? And it seems to me that the Jerusalem version written in the books is the main one, and so I received it in tractate Makkot (19a): “If he holds it sanctified for the future, let him be in doubt about the firstborn too; and if he holds it did not sanctify, let him not be in doubt about tithe either. Actually, he holds it sanctified for the future, and here, where the firstborn is obvious to him, it is such as one whose blood was sprinkled in the presence of the Temple, and so on.” And we do not read “since if the blood were there, it would not be subject to sprinkling, and so on”; rather, we read: “And the meat comes and is derived from the blood: just as its blood at the altar, so its meat at the altar.” That is, just as the blood of this one was sprinkled in the time of the altar, so its meat is eaten only in the time of the altar; and tithe comes and learns from this meat.
gershom:b1.1: And do we derive sacred things from one another? But it says in tractate Zevaḥim: in the entire Torah we derive a derived thing from a derived thing, except for sacred things. And this tithe and firstborn are sacred things, and its meat is derived from their blood; how then is tithe derived from its meat, which is itself derived?
gershom:b2.1: [Grain] tithe is non-sacred, since one can deconsecrate it and eat it anywhere.
gershom:b3.1: This works out well according to the one who says we follow the derived: if the derived is a sacred thing, we do not derive from a derived thing; and if the derived is non-sacred, deriving from a derived thing is fine, and this derived thing, tithe, is non-sacred. But according to the one who says we follow the teaching source, what is there to say? For the teaching source is its meat, which is sacred; how can one derive from a teaching source that is sacred?
gershom:b4.1: This is not a case of a derived thing from a derived thing, since meat and blood are one matter, and tithe can be derived from it.
gershom:b5.1: Another version: actually, he holds the initial consecration did not sanctify for the future, and here it is a firstborn whose blood was sprinkled in the presence of the Temple, and the Temple was destroyed, and its meat still exists. Since, if the blood were still here after the destruction, [like the meat,] it would not be subject to sprinkling, since there is no Temple, that sprinkling counts for nothing; and the [meat] comes and is derived from the blood: just as the blood’s sprinkling does not count, so too the meat has no remedy. And tithe comes and is derived from the firstborn; and do we derive, and so on. And this other version did not seem reasonable to my teacher; rather, he said the first is the main one, for so we find it written in tractate Makkot.
rashi:b3.1: Grain tithe comes only from the Land: in the first chapter of Kiddushin, at its end (36b).
rashi:b3.2: You bring up a firstborn: and the baraita that they did not accept from ben Antigonus is Rabbi Akiva’s, and our mishna is Rabbi Yishmael’s, for whom this verse is not free for this exposition.
tosafot:b4.1: From a place that you do not bring up grain tithe, you do not bring up a firstborn: now we have found the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yishmael holds that ab initio one does not bring a firstborn and a tithe animal from outside the Land to the Land, but after the fact, if they came unblemished they are sacrificed, which is like our mishna; and Rabbi Akiva holds that even after the fact they are not sacrificed, since it is juxtaposed to grain tithe, and the case of ben Antigonus follows his view. And if you ask: granted Rabbi Akiva, whose reason is explained, that the firstborn is juxtaposed to grain tithe; but according to Rabbi Yishmael, what is the reason? If he holds the juxtaposition to grain tithe, then even after the fact no; and if he does not hold it, then even ab initio let him bring it! One can answer that he derives it from the exposition of the Sifrei explained above: “Only your sacred things which you have…” (Deuteronomy 12:26) — from here that one brings sacred things from outside the Land to the Land. One might think that the firstborn and the tithe animal are the same; therefore it says “only.” And it excludes only ab initio, since that is what the verse speaks of, as it is written: “you shall take and come,” which is ab initio.
rashi:b5.1: In any place that overlooks: any place that one standing in Jerusalem can see.
tosafot:b5.1: One might have thought that a person may bring up second tithe and eat it, and so on: And if you ask: why would we have thought it may be eaten in any place that overlooks? “Before the Lord your God” is written of it! One can answer: like Shiloh, where they ate second tithe in any place that overlooks. And there are books that have this question and this answer in the text.
gershom:b6.1: Ben Azzai says: one might have thought a person may bring second tithe in the time of the Temple and eat it.
gershom:b7.1: In any place that overlooks: in any place from which one can see Jerusalem.
rashi:b5.2: And it is a logical inference: that it is not eaten [there].
rashi:b5.3: Just as a firstborn is eaten only within the wall: since sacred things are disqualified by leaving [their area].
rashi:b5.4: What about the firstborn, which you distinguished in the time of its eating and in those who eat it? [Rashi’s text of the refutation reads so, where ours has “which requires placing of blood and sacrificial portions on the altar.”] You distinguished in the time of its eating, since it is eaten only for two days and one night, and second tithe forever; and you distinguished in those who eat it, since it is eaten only by priests, and second tithe by any person.
gershom:b8.1: Just as a firstborn is eaten only within the wall, as we learned: and they are eaten throughout the city by any person. [Rabbeinu Gershom, like Rashi, reads the refutation:] Since you distinguished in it the time of its eating and those who eat it: for an unblemished firstborn is eaten only for two days and one night, and is eaten only by priests, while second tithe has no time limit and is eaten by any person.
rashi:b7.1: And what is difficult for him: for ben Azzai, who says “one might have thought,” and so on. And where would you get this idea, that it may be eaten in any place that overlooks, that a verse was needed for it?
gershom:b9.1: And what is difficult, that we say “one might have thought”? That is, why would it enter our minds that tithe may be eaten in any place that overlooks? This is difficult for him because:
rashi:b7.2: And in Jerusalem, within the wall: and it is difficult for him: granted, offerings of lesser sanctity require placing of blood; but let tithe be eaten in any place that overlooks. [The verse] teaches us [otherwise].
gershom:b10.1: For we learned: there is no difference between Shiloh, and so on: for there it was eaten in any place that overlooks, because it was an open village that had no wall.
gershom:b11.1: Granted, a firstborn requires a wall, since it is written: “And you shall eat before the Lord your God,” in a sacred place.
rashi:b9.1: And be disqualified: from sacrifice, since it is written “year by year” (Deuteronomy 15:20).
gershom:b12.1: A firstborn whose year has passed: since it is written: “Before the Lord your God you shall eat it year by year” (Deuteronomy 15:20).
gershom:b13.1: Just as second tithe is not disqualified from one year to the next: for at any time one can redeem it and bring it up. And the earlier tanna’im are the three elders.
rashi:b11.1: Year by year: seven years are implied.
rashi:b12.1: One day of this year: that he slaughtered it as commanded at the end of its year, and the verse teaches us that it is eaten that day and the next day, which is of the other year.
rashi:b13.1: Like the breast of the waving: that is, the breast and thigh of peace offerings, which are eaten for two days and one night. [Another version:] “It shall be… and their meat shall be yours, like the breast of the waving”: for presumably we would go to the stringent side and say (Zevaḥim 57a) “like the breast and thigh of the thanks offering,” and it is written “it shall be” to add another “being” like it, and that is the second day.
gershom:b14.1: They derive [that it is eaten for two days and one night] from “But the firstborn of an ox…” (Numbers 18:17), and next to it, “And their meat shall be yours, like the breast of the waving and like the right thigh” (Numbers 18:18). And we say in tractate Bekhorot: then say “like the breast and thigh of the thanks offering,” which is eaten for a day and a night; that is why at its end it [again] writes “it shall be yours,” for the verse added for you one more “being,” a second day. From here, that it is eaten for two days and one night.
gershom:b16.1: The offspring of a sin offering, and so on, and one whose year passed or that was lost: if he did not manage to sacrifice it [until its year passed, or] until it was lost and found blemished, or until its owner achieved atonement with another, in either case it shall die.
gershom:b17.1: And they do not render a substitute: this one that was found, since it was sanctified not with inherent sanctity but with sanctity of value.
rashi:b15.1: MISHNA. And that was lost and found blemished: before he achieved atonement with another.
rashi:b15.2: If the owner achieved atonement: afterward, with another.
rashi:b15.3: It shall die: even according to the Rabbis, who say below, disagreeing with Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], that a sin offering dies only when it is found after the owner achieved atonement, in this case they agree, since there are two detriments: it was lost and it was found blemished. And that is why it mentions “blemished”: for if it were unblemished, since it was found before atonement, even if the owner later achieved atonement with another, it grazes.
tosafot:b15.1: MISHNA. The offspring of a sin offering… and that was lost and found blemished: Rashi explained: even according to the Rabbis, who say below, disagreeing with Rabbi, that a sin offering dies only when found after the owner achieved atonement, here they agree, since there are two detriments, lost and found blemished; and that is why it mentions “blemished,” for if unblemished, since it was found before atonement, even if the owner later achieved atonement with another, it grazes. End of his words. And this is not clear, for his explanation implies that more detriments bring it to death, while on the contrary the discussion in our Gemara implies that more detriments bring it to grazing, as Rava says in the Gemara: an animal lost at night is not considered lost, meaning it does not die but grazes. And further, according to Rabbi Abba, who says in the Gemara below (Temurah 23a) that all agree that if he achieved atonement with one that was not lost, the lost one dies — and here it deals with one who achieved atonement with one that was not lost — if so, why do I need “blemished” according to Rabbi Abba? However, there are discussions in the chapter Mi SheHaya Tamei (Pesaḥim 97a), in the chapter HaToda (Menaḥot 80a), and below too (Temurah 23a) that do not hold like Rabbi Abba. And further, the Gemara below infers from the next clause of the mishna that the mishna is the Rabbis’; it could have inferred it from here, from its mentioning “blemished.” Therefore it seems to explain that it mentions “blemished” to teach a novelty: lest you say that since it was so diminished, both lost and blemished, it is like an animal lost at night and it grazes, it teaches us that even so it dies.
tosafot:b15.2: If the owner achieved atonement, it shall die: each master according to his view: according to Rabbi, even if it was found before atonement; according to the Rabbis, when it was found after atonement.
